answers.answer: No. SCOPe groups all three only at the fold level, not as one superfamily. In SCOPe 2.08, class f (membrane and cell-surface proteins) contains fold f.21 "Heme-binding four-helical bundle" (sunid 81344). Its curator comment describes the core as four transmembrane helices in an up-and-down bundle, with one or two hemes bound between the helices. That fold has three separate superfamilies: f.21.1 Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes (sunid 81342), f.21.2 Fumarate reductase respiratory complex transmembrane subunits (sunid 81343), and f.21.3 Respiratory nitrate reductase 1 gamma chain (sunid 103501). In SCOPe, a shared fold only means the proteins have the same arrangement of secondary-structure elements. It does not establish common ancestry. Placing them in separate superfamilies means SCOPe did not find enough structural, functional or sequence evidence to call them probable homologs. The similarity could come from convergent evolution, because membrane-spanning helix bundles that hold heme are physically constrained. Distant homology is not ruled out, but SCOPe does not claim it, so treating these groups as one homologous superfamily goes beyond what SCOPe supports. It is also unsafe to transfer specifics between them, such as heme count, heme ligands, redox partners, quinone-site details, or functional annotations, or to treat one as an evolutionary template for another, just because they share the fold. A structural template chosen only for the shared helix-bundle shape is a fold-level template, not evidence of homology. To argue that any two of them are homologous, you would need evidence beyond fold membership. Examples are significant sequence similarity from profile or HMM searches, conserved heme-ligand and quinone-site motifs at matching positions, structural similarity well beyond the generic four-helix core (such as FATCAT or DALI scores combined with matching unusual features), and agreement with independent classifications such as Pfam clans or ECOD. SCOPe's own grouping supports only a shared fold.
